10.1002_smsc.70431: Group III–V semiconductors are suitable for solar‐driven hydrogen production due to precise lattice matching (for tandem device combinations), high carrier mobilities (>10 3 cm 2 V –1 s –1 ), tunable bandgaps (1.1–2.5 eV), strong absorption coefficients (>10 5 cm –1 ), and a large range of doping possibilities. GaInP 2 , GaAs, and InP have a theoretical solar‐to‐hydrogen efficiency of more than 20%. Still, their high susceptibility to chemical and photochemical corrosion during prolonged photoelectrochemical water splitting (PEC‐WS) is a major industrial hurdle. This review comprehensively covers critical strategies to enhance the photostability of group III–V semiconductors for industrial‐scale PEC‐WS, emphasizing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) support. We discuss three main intrinsic and extrinsic strategies that include (i) AI‐driven crystal structure modification and faceted growth control, (ii) physical and chemical surface passivation coupled with machine learning for passivation material screening strategies, and (iii) combining III–V semiconductors with appropriate band‐aligned materials via preferable heterojunctions, utilizing algorithms to select optimal compositions. We examine the underlying mechanisms of each strategy and conclude with perspectives on achieving optimal materials for PEC‐WS using advanced AI and ML screening tools. Implementing these effective modification strategies, the wide commercial potential of III–V photoelectrodes for PEC‐WS technology can be unlocked.
10.1016_j.est.2026.123855: Lithium-ion batteries are a key energy-storage technology for electromobility due to their high specific and volumetric energy densities. As electric vehicles are required to meet stringent performance and safety standards comparable to those of combustion engine systems, the early detection of safety-critical failure mechanisms in battery cells is becoming increasingly important. When lithium-ion cells are operated outside their designated safe operating window due to electrical, thermal, mechanical or chemical stress, various degradation processes can be triggered, potentially leading to thermal runaway. To mitigate these risks, in-situ monitoring techniques capable of identifying early indicators of abnormal cell behavior are of particular interest. This review paper presents a comprehensive and application-oriented overview of current early warning methods for thermal runaway detection in lithium-ion batteries. The focus is placed on sensor-based approaches at the single-cell level, structured according to electrical, thermal, chemical and mechanical detection principles. The reviewed approaches are systematically evaluated with respect to their applicability in automotive battery systems, considering criteria such as thermal runaway detectability, integration feasibility, robustness, energy efficiency and cost efficiency. The aim of this work is to identify promising sensing strategies that can improve battery safety by enabling the early detection of hazardous operating states.
10.1016_j.watres.2026.126180: Seawater requires pretreatment before reverse osmosis (SWRO) to minimize membrane fouling, but conventional methods increase energy use and chemical consumption, and their robustness when feedwater quality fluctuates is low. Ultrafiltration (UF) offers a promising alternative, producing higher-quality permeate, tolerating feedwater variability, and lowering chemical use; however, UF membranes still suffer from fouling during seawater treatment. Polyzwitterionic (PZI) brushes grafted onto porous membranes show excellent antifouling in water treatment, but their application in seawater pretreatment remains unexplored. Here, poly(sulfobetaine methacrylate) (polySBMA) brushes were grafted onto polyethersulfone UF membranes via atom transfer radical polymerization and evaluated using real seawater (RSW) supplemented with dissolved organic carbon derived from seawater algae. Surface analysis confirmed successful grafting, with brush thickness increasing with polymerization time (1-12 h). Quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation (QCM-D) and atomic force microscopy showed that brush swelling increased in Milli-Q water and more in seawater. Fouling tests with the DOC-enriched RSW demonstrated improved antifouling relative to unmodified membranes, dependent on brush thickness. Membranes grafted for 6 h operated stably for 8 days at 95% water recovery, with only a 1.42-fold transmembrane pressure increase, whereas unmodified UF membranes doubled TMP within 24 h. QCM-D and post-fouling membrane analyses confirmed the antifouling effects of the polySBMA brushes. Seawater quality after pretreatment met standards for RO feedwater. RO desalination of pretreated seawater remained stable over 12 h, demonstrating that the grafted membranes of the present study are also effective in reducing fouling, thereby enhancing the overall robustness of the SWRO process.
